reading.body:
Omnicell is a hospital medication automation company, not an AI compute company, and its data shows no connection to data centers, power, or the grid.

The record is a standard public-company footprint: eight SEC filings between February and August 2026, a Texas headquarters, and 68 granted patents since 2001. The recent patents cover syringe cap loading, temperature-controlled dispense drawers, IV compounding, and parallel preparation processing. That is robotics and refrigeration for pharmacy workflows, which is physical automation of a different kind than the GPU-dense facilities this site tracks.

The one thread that touches the thesis is indirect. Automated dispensing cabinets, IV compounding robots, and medication packaging lines are hospital equipment that runs on building power and must stay available, so the company sits on the demand side of the same grid that constrains AI. Nothing in the data quantifies that load, and no filing here reports energy use, so the link should not be pushed further than it goes.

What the data does not cover is substantial. There are no products listed, no AI cases, no data center or power agreements, and no financial figures. The 126 count under Texas law exposure is a state-level tally with no detail on what it counts. A reader should treat this as a company identity and patent record, not as evidence about AI infrastructure.

profile_text.body:
Omnicell is a healthcare technology company headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas. It makes automated medication management systems for hospitals, plus adherence packaging and patient engagement software for retail pharmacies, sold under the Omnicell and EnlivenHealth brands.

Source: Wikipedia, Omnicell, retrieved 22 September 2026.
